title: The Qubit Budget
primary_metric: dollars of cloud-quantum compute cost per successfully-completed (below-error-threshold) shot, for a 20-qubit register vs. a 24-qubit register solving the same client routing problem

options.A: The Near-Term Register — commit to 20 qubits, cheaper and inside budget, but its 2^20 state space can't fully represent the client's 24-variable problem, forcing a classical-heuristic approximation on 4 lanes
options.B: The Full Register — commit to 24 qubits, whose 2^24 state space (16x larger) represents the client's problem exactly, but real published hardware error rates compound faster as circuit width grows, and cloud-quantum time is billed per shot regardless of whether that shot lands below the error threshold

deliverables.text: A state-space computation: evaluate 2^20 and 2^24 exactly, compute the ratio 2^24 / 2^20 as a single power of 2, and use it to explain why only the 24-qubit register represents all 24 of the client's decision variables at once.
A circuit gate-count table: using Appendix D's calibrated gate-count model, compute the number of two-qubit gates required at 20 qubits and at 24 qubits.
A below-threshold success-probability computation: evaluate (1 - gate error rate)^(number of two-qubit gates) for both register sizes, following order of operations (parentheses before exponent).

A cost-per-successful-shot table and margin: using D3's success probabilities and Appendix E's per-shot price, compute dollars per successfully-completed shot for both options and the percent margin between them.
A recommendation memo defended with D1's exact state-space comparison, D4's cost-per-successful-shot numbers and margin, and Appendix A's fact about the 4 uncovered lanes under Option A.

appendices.title: The Client's Routing Problem & Latticeworks' Constraints
Option A — The Near-Term Register (20 Qubits)
Option B — The Full Register (24 Qubits)
IonQ Forte — Published Hardware Error Data & Gate-Count Model

balance.argument_a: The Near-Term Register is real cost efficient: at IonQ Forte's real, published median two-qubit gate error rate (0.464%, S2), the smaller circuit width means fewer two-qubit gates (200 vs. 240 under the case's calibrated gate-count model), a higher below-threshold success probability (0.3945 vs. 0.3275), and a genuinely lower dollars-per-successful-shot figure ($0.2028 vs. $0.2443) -- a real, sourced 17.0% margin. It also fits comfortably inside this quarter's budget (Appendix A).
balance.argument_b: The Full Register is the only option that represents the client's actual 24-variable problem exactly -- the Near-Term Register's cheaper successful shots are shots that only solve 20 of the client's 24 decision variables, leaving 4 lanes to an un-costed, un-sourced classical fallback heuristic (Appendix A, MA3) whose own error is not captured anywhere in D4's numbers. A cheaper wrong-shaped answer is not obviously a better deal than a costlier exactly-shaped one, especially for a client contract, and the 24-qubit register's real state-space exactness (2^24, Appendix C) is a permanent representational guarantee the 20-qubit register structurally cannot offer at any price.
balance.margin_basis: Compute dollars per successfully-completed shot for each register size: price-per-shot (identical for both options, S1, so it cancels out of the margin entirely) divided by the below-error-threshold success probability (1 - gate_error_rate)^(gates(N)), where gates(N) is the case's calibrated linear gate-count model (MA5, gates(N) = 10*N, calibrated to S2's real anchor of ~200 two-qubit gates at width ~20). Margin is the percent difference between the two options' cost-per-successful-shot.
balance.margin_note: COMPUTED 2026-09-01 (case-research). gate_error_rate = 0.00464 (S2, real median two-qubit gate error, IonQ Forte). gates(20) = 10*20 = 200 (matches S2's real stated anchor exactly). gates(24) = 10*24 = 240 (MA5, linear extrapolation from the same real anchor). F(20) = (1-0.00464)^200 = 0.394491. F(24) = (1-0.00464)^240 = 0.327525. price_per_shot = $0.08 (S1, identical for both options -- IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL FINDING: price_per_shot cancels completely out of margin_pct, since cost(N) = price/F(N) and margin_pct = 1 - F(B)/F(A)*... -- the winner and the margin depend ONLY on the register-size-dependent success probability, never on the per-shot price. A cheaper or more expensive cloud-compute vendor would change the absolute dollar figures but never flip the recommendation or change the margin at all.) cost(20) = 0.08/0.394491 = $0.202793. cost(24) = 0.08/0.327525 = $0.244256. margin_pct = (0.244256-0.202793)/0.244256*100 = 16.975% (rounded 16.98%). WINNER: Option A, The Near-Term Register. This margin is comfortably inside SPEC §2's ~20% cap -- no retune or waiver needed. COUNTERFACTUAL MODEL-SENSITIVITY CHECK (logged for transparency, per case-research practice on prior cases): if the gate-count model instead used IonQ's own #AQ worst-case formula (gates = N^2, i.e. 400 at N=20 and 576 at N=24) rather than the case's calibrated-anchor linear model (MA5), F(20) = 0.155623, F(24) = 0.068641, cost(20) = $0.514063, cost(24) = $1.165478, margin_pct = 55.9% -- still Option A cheaper, but no longer a close race, and well past the ~20% cap. This case deliberately uses the linear, anchor-calibrated model (directly matching S2's own stated real number at width~20, and consistent with S2's own real application-circuit examples showing sub-quadratic gate counts) rather than the n^2 worst-case formula, and states this modeling choice explicitly as MA5 with its sensitivity flagged HIGH in case.md's Modeling Assumptions block. Both models agree on the WINNER (Option A); they disagree sharply on how CLOSE the race is.

Gate-count model: gates(N) = 10 x N two-qubit gates
modeling_assumptions.value: 200 gates at N=20 (exact match to S2's real anchor); 240 gates at N=24 (extrapolated)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Calibrated so the model exactly reproduces S2's own stated real anchor (~200 two-qubit gates sustainable at width ~20 before crossing the 1/e #AQ threshold), then extended linearly to N=24.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: HIGH -- the single most margin-determining modeling choice in the case. Using IonQ's own #AQ worst-case formula (gates = N^2) instead would raise the margin from ~17.0% to ~55.9% (see balance.margin_note for the full counterfactual). Both models agree Option A wins; they disagree sharply on how close the race is.

sensitivity_note: margin_pct (16.98%) is computed from a real median gate-error rate (S2) and a gate-count model (MA5) calibrated to S2's own stated real anchor -- it comfortably clears SPEC §2's ~20% cap with no retune needed. The single largest lever on the margin is MA5 (the gate-count-vs-register-size scaling model): the alternative real, defensible n^2 (#AQ worst-case) scaling would put the margin at ~55.9% instead -- still the same winner, but a much less close race. Per-shot price (S1) is NOT a lever at all: it is identical for both options and cancels completely out of margin_pct, so a different cloud-compute vendor's pricing would change the absolute dollar figures shown in Appendix E but never the winner or the margin. See sensitivity_model.py for a runnable sweep of gate_error_rate and the gate-count model's slope.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA5's calibrated linear gate-count model (10 gates/qubit) is directly anchored to S2's real stated anchor at width~=20 (~200 two-qubit gates); the case.json balance.margin_note documents that swapping to IonQ's own n^2 worst-case formula (the Twist) still keeps Option A winning but widens the margin from ~17.0% to ~55.9%, i.e. flexing the effective per-gate error assumption moves the margin, never the winner, in every reading tested.

Same MA5 calibrated-anchor model; case.md's own Modeling Assumptions block flags MA5's sensitivity as HIGH and documents the counterfactual n^2 formula explicitly (margin 17.0% -> 55.9%, winner unchanged). This is a disclosed, not hidden, modeling-choice sensitivity.
